item.title: Palantir postpones recruitment event following community backlash
item.dc:creator: Audrey Adam and Arleny Flores
item.description: Approximately 100 members of the College community gathered in front of Mears House last Friday to protest a Palantir Technologies recruiting event that had been set to be hosted by the ’68 Center for Career Exploration that afternoon.
item.content:encoded:
Approximately 100 members of the College community gathered in front of Mears House last Friday to protest a Palantir Technologies recruiting event that had been set to be hosted by the ’68 Center for Career Exploration that afternoon. The protest was organized by a group of students at the College under the name of the Concerned Students’ Collective (CSC), who started a petition against the event after learning about it from a promotional email sent to students by the ’68 Center on Nov. 9.

“Interested in seeing how software creates real-world impact? Join us for an exclusive, interactive session with Palantir Technologies on Friday, November 13th,” the email read. “Whether you’re looking to dive into technical demos or network casually over coffee and pizza, you’ll have the opportunity to connect 1-on-1 with Palantir deployment strategists and forward-deployed software engineers.”

Palantir informed students who registered for the event that it would be postponed due to “unforeseen circumstances” in a Thursday morning email.

Palantir is a U.S.-based company specializing in data analytics and artificial intelligence (AI). The company has been criticized for its contracts with government entities including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Israeli Defense Forces.

Students organize against Palantir’s planned visit to campus

The CSC released a statement alongside its petition, titled “Not in Our Name­ – No to Palantir at Williams,” the same day that the ’68 Center sent their promotional email to students.

“We cannot in good conscience stand by as the College lures students towards jobs that require them to compromise their morals and do so without context,” the statement read.

According to an email that the CSC sent to petition signers last Thursday, the petition received more than 800 signatures and 400 comments within the first 36 hours of its publication. Petition signers include students, current College staff, alums, and faculty members, according to an email that the CSC sent to protest signers on Tuesday afternoon.

In addition to the efforts of the CSC, which included pasting posters across campus, Associate Professor of English Bernie Rhie shared the petition in an Instagram post on Nov. 11. “By giving them a platform, the College isn’t simply allowing a company to use a space on campus,” his caption read. “It’s lending its institutional credibility to a company and helping it recruit our students into its workforce… If you, too, are appalled, please consider signing a petition started by two current students to express our collective anger that this event is being allowed to happen.”

In their Thursday email, the CSC also wrote that they had met with members of the College administration to discuss their opposition to the event. “[We held] meetings with President Maud S. Mandel and a significant portion of the ’68 Center’s board, where we delivered the petition, your comments, our non-negotiables, and our goals for the future,” they wrote.

Mandel addressed community response to the Palantir recruitment session in a statement to the Record. “When there’s controversy on campus, I see it as an opportunity to do what liberal arts communities like Williams do so well: consider the ideas at stake; ask how different approaches might (or might not) serve our values, goals and needs; and engage in serious, open debate about the options,” she wrote. “I’ll never commit to making policy decisions before such a discussion has even been had. What I will promise is that my colleagues and I will listen carefully to the full range of views. These are some of the most intellectually stimulating conversations I get to have as president, and I welcome anyone who is interested in sharing their ideas and opinions with us,” Mandel wrote.

In their Thursday email, the CSC also recommended that petition signers call or email the ’68 Center or the President’s Office to voice their dissatisfaction with the Palantir recruiting event. They included a call script and email template for interested petitioners.

Simon Huffman ’24 called the ’68 Center on Thursday morning, but their voicemail box was already full. “The Career Center didn’t pick up, and I got a recording that their voice box was full and not taking any more messages,” he wrote to the Record.

After hearing the next day that the event would be postponed, the CSC sent another email to petition signers announcing that the protest would continue as planned. “A postponement means that [the College and ’68 Center] are waiting for this to die down,” it read. “We won’t let that happen.”

In a statement to the Record, ’68 Center Executive Director Don Kjelleren wrote that “the decision to postpone [the event] was Palantir’s.” His statement also said that the proposed one-on-one meetings for the 54 students who registered for the event were moved online.

The CSC also outlined its demands to the College in their email to petition signers on Thursday. “We need tangible guarantees that it won’t happen again and that the College’s ties with Palantir, including any Winter Study courses connected to the company, are revoked,” it read.

The annual Winter Study course CCE 42: “Exploring Careers,” organized by the ’68 Center, has brought students to meet with alums working at Palantir, among other companies, during its past trips to New York. The course most recently brought students to the company’s office in 2025. Kjelleren also noted that Palantir conducted an on-campus information session for students last year.

The CSC’s email read, “We also want to know how this was approved without opposition, why it was promoted to students without any context, and why no administrator has been willing to take any responsibility.”

“This goes far beyond Palantir. It’s students who are asked to compromise on their morals when we’re given half the information, and the College makes accommodations for companies like this. That’s why we want real student involvement in decisions about events like this from now on,” the email continued. “Our non-negotiables: firm guarantees about Palantir and no policy change without substantial, non-symbolic student involvement. We’re also meeting with the administration about potential frameworks for handling events like this in the future, and we’d love your feedback.”

The email said that the CSC has been working with a group unaffiliated with the College called the Action Center for Corporate Accountability (ACCA) on these frameworks. The website of the ACCA’s parent organization, the American Friends Service Committee, states that “[the] ACCA helps movements engage with large corporations on a moral equal footing, build leverage to change corporate policies and practices, and limit political influence and reach.”

Students and faculty protest

Shortly after 2 p.m. on Friday — the recruitment session’s original starting time — Basim Mutaal ’27, an organizer with the CSC, opened the protest with a speech explaining the CSC’s demands before leading chants and kicking off a lineup of speakers.

In his speech, Professor of Political Science James Mahon called on the College to establish procedures for evaluating employers before inviting them to recruit. “We have to make an institutional adjustment,” he said. “The kinds of changes you guys are proposing, where companies get vetted ahead of time, would mean that students don’t have to face a choice between getting a job and giving up their principles every time a recruiter shows up on campus.”

After Mahon, Associate Professor of Sociology Ben Snyder, a scholar of surveillance technology, spoke. He said that Palantir exists in the broader “surveillance capitalism” industry, describing how companies profit by commoditizing information about individuals. “Data is a word we use to guard ourselves emotionally from looking at the fact that what is being mined by these companies is information about our humanity,” he said.

Snyder also said the College failed to address the implications of Palantir’s work. “When Williams invites our students to pursue careers with a company like Palantir, [their work] is what we are sanctioning,” he said. “That is what we roll out the red carpet for.”

After Snyder spoke, local organizer Hari Kumar addressed the crowd. Kumar is a small business owner who has previously served as an adjunct professor in the dance department and taught Winter Study courses in theater. He called on students to speak on behalf of those who could not voice their opinions. “There are staff members here and workers here who have been told that they cannot show up here and be openly in support of what you are doing,” he said. “Remind them that they are not alone because we are not alone.”

Kumar told the Record that he has organized events and workshops about his business on campus in the past, but solely by invitation from a College office or department. “This is no different than any organization that wants to come to campus and ask for some kind of official space,” he said in an interview with the Record. “I’m a small business owner, I do communications skills training. If I wanted to come and do an event on campus, I’d have to get approval from … a campus [office] in some way. I can’t just roll up, put up a table, and broadcast whatever I want to students.”

Visiting Professor in Democratic Studies Sonja Drimmer followed Kumar’s speech at the protest. Drimmer pointed out that the College’s values contrast with statements from Palantir’s chief executive officer, Alex Karp. “If Williams’ statement is that this is an inclusive community, then Palantir has no place here,” she said.

Sayer Theiss ’29, another CSC organizer, then spoke about the similarities between Friday’s protest and the student body’s opposition to the CIA’s recruitment efforts at the College in 1969. “Fifty-seven years ago, the Career Center was still refusing to abandon their facilitation of a pipeline transforming Williams students, supposedly the best and brightest, the supposed leaders of tomorrow, into conduits for oppression and the profiteers of war and surveillance,” he said. “Take away 57 years, nothing is different. They’re doing the exact same thing.”

After Theiss, organizers offered the microphone to the crowd, inviting attendees to share their thoughts. Several students voiced their concerns about Palantir’s partnerships. Others shared their personal experiences with ICE and called on the College to more stringently vet who is allowed to recruit on campus.

At the end of the march, organizers led the crowd through Frosh Quad and in front of Sawyer Library. As protesters hung a banner that said “Palantir Kills,” the crowd chanted phrases such as “No purple pride in genocide” and “We won’t use our minds to commit war crimes.” Organizers thanked attendees and asked them to look out for next steps.

“This is also the beginning of a campaign,” Addis Cone ’27, also a CSC organizer, said at the protest. “We are going to be strategic. We’re going to make sure that Palantir, even though postponed, can never come here again.”

’68 Center responds to student demands

The ’68 Center’s decision to host the event was based on its adherence to the National Association of College and Employers (NACE) Principles for Ethical Professional Practice, Kjelleren said. “Most of us have strong negative personal reactions to specific organizations and our instinct is to block and tackle them,” he wrote. “Those feelings are real and often justified. The problem is if we replace free choice with censorship, someone will have to decide who has access, and who doesn’t.”

According to Kjelleren, any changes or augmentations to NACE would have to go through the association directly. “The national NACE standards have been adopted by almost 2000 colleges, and changing them would involve working directly with NACE through its governance structure,” he wrote.

Kjelleren added that the ’68 Center is willing to discuss students’ proposed changes or additions to NACE standards. “We are always open to suggestions,” he wrote.

He did not provide a definitive answer on whether the Palantir event would be rescheduled or permanently canceled. “Our policies and our commitment to NACE haven’t changed,” Kjelleren wrote in an email to the Record. “Hosting a recruiting event is not an endorsement of a company or its practices. Students are free to pursue opportunities that interest them, just as they’re free to express their disagreement with companies they oppose.”

item.title: As FAST budget runs low, members plan constitutional reforms
item.dc:creator: Soren Anderson-Flynn
item.description: The Facilitators for Allocating Student Taxes (FAST) have allocated approximately 90 percent of their estimated annual budget as of yesterday, leaving $42,813.30 remaining for the 2026-27 academic year. FAST facilitators cited structural issues in their constitution and large budget requests from Registered Student Organizations (RSOs) as being responsible for the shortage, while members of the College administration have argued that the high spending itself is unconstitutional. In response to the budgetary issues, FAST has paused supplemental budget funding and facilitators are planning constitutional change.
item.content:encoded:
The Facilitators for Allocating Student Taxes (FAST) have allocated approximately 90 percent of their estimated annual budget as of yesterday, leaving $42,813.30 remaining for the 2026-27 academic year. FAST facilitators cited structural issues in their constitution and large budget requests from Registered Student Organizations (RSOs) as being responsible for the shortage, while members of the College administration have argued that the high spending itself is unconstitutional. In response to the budgetary issues, FAST has paused supplemental budget funding and facilitators are planning constitutional change.

FAST is an elected body composed of five student members who allocate funds from the Student Activities Tax — a part of every student’s tuition — to RSOs. Each September, FAST receives an estimate of the academic year’s total Student Activities Tax. This year, it was $427,689.95. Of that total, approximately $120,000 was automatically allocated to All Campus Entertainment (ACE) and $34,000 was allocated to the Williams Outing Club (WOC), which are outside of FAST’s purview.

RSOs are divided into six sectors: ACE, WOC, Minority Coalition (MinCo) groups, competitive teams, performance groups, and at-large student organizations. Each sector is awarded a fixed percentage of that year’s estimated FAST budget.

Currently serving on FAST are MinCo facilitator Sahil Sajid ’29, competitive teams facilitator Gavin Aurelus ’29, performance groups facilitator Jack Allen Greenfield ’27, and at-large members Annabel Smith ’29 and Emma Guo ’29.

RSO treasurers submit annual budget requests to FAST at the beginning of each year, when the majority of funding is allocated, and can submit supplemental requests throughout the year. According to the FAST constitution, facilitators can only distribute up to 90 percent of a sector’s total allocations in the annual budget process. FAST exceeded the 90 percent threshold for both MinCo and performance groups this year, leaving less than 10 percent of funds available for supplemental requests.

According to FAST facilitators, many RSOs requested more money than they received last year. “RSO treasurers have been requesting larger amounts of money than their audits have stated they needed in years prior,” Greenfield said in an interview with the Record in which he said he was speaking on behalf of FAST.

FAST facilitators cited the increased budget requests as one of the main factors behind FAST’s low funds. The other factor, according to the facilitators, was a renewed emphasis by members of the College administration on the language in FAST’s constitution that limits facilitators’ ability to deny funding requests. “It was emphasized by an administrator to us, both in person and over email, that budgets could only be rejected if they violate the [FAST] constitution,” Greenfield said. “As such, we followed the direct orders of the administration.”

FAST facilitators do not have free reign to deny funds to RSOs. One of the functions of FAST is to “approve all funding requests that adhere to the bounds and principles outlined in this Constitution,” according to the FAST constitution. These principles restrict how RSOs can use FAST funding.

Assistant Director for Student Involvement Trevor Biggs, who currently serves as FAST’s interim advisor, confirmed that he discouraged facilitators from outright denying many funding requests. “When meeting with FAST, I have emphasized that their constitution provides very few mechanisms to deny a funding request that meets FAST’s community standards,” he wrote in an email to the Record.

However, Biggs added that he cited FAST’s constitutional provisions on overspending when meeting with facilitators. “Attributing FAST’s high spending to that guidance leaves out the second half of the constitutional framework that [the FAST advisory board] also emphasized, which set limits on funding allocations for annual budgets and the fall semester,” he wrote. Specifically, the constitution prohibits using more than 90 percent of sector allocations on annual budgets and allocating more than 60 percent of supplemental funds during the fall semester.

“I identified to FAST that initial annual budget approvals in both the Performance and MinCo sectors had exceeded the total funds available in those pools, which violated the FAST constitution’s 90 percent annual allocation cap, ” Biggs added.

FAST facilitators said that confusing directives from administrators prevented them from carrying out all of their mandates. They cited one email from an administrator which read, “Anticipating future budget scarcity is not grounds to reject a supplemental budget request.”

Some RSO treasurers have expressed frustration with their interactions with FAST. “From our first ever funding request … I had a poor impression from FAST due to a lack of timely response, and clear communication regarding the status of funding requests,” Eniola Olabode ’27, treasurer for the Black Student Union, wrote in an email to the Record.

FAST facilitators said that multiple other confounding factors have interfered with their ability to communicate with RSOs and consistently allocate funds.

The program that FAST uses to log their finances, track funding requests, and communicate with treasurers malfunctioned during the period when many groups requested their annual budgets, according to the FAST facilitators. “Our Google automated system, such as our emails, our Google Sheets, and our website, broke,” Greenfield said. “We lost ownership over them and could no longer edit parts of them. We also could not automate any of our previously automated processes, such as sending out budget approvals via a simple click.” These systems are now functional, he added.

The facilitators — all five of whom are new to FAST this academic year — also said that they did not receive any training for the position from the administration or outgoing FAST members.

FAST’s master spreadsheet, which is publicly available, confirms that annual allocations have exceeded the total allotted sector allocations for MinCo and performance groups. MinCo restructured at the beginning of the academic year, designating MinCo groups as either “core” or “affiliate” and preventing affiliate groups from requesting annual budgets from MinCo, requiring them to request annual funding directly from FAST. This change increased the financial pressure FAST faced during the annual budgeting process, according to FAST facilitators.

Members of the College administration proposed that FAST cut a level percentage of all MinCo and performance group annual budgets to bring them back under the cap of 90 percent of their respective sector allocations, according to Biggs. “Based on FAST’s current budget figures, we calculated that the accurate adjustments required by their own constitution are approximately 13.7 percent for MinCo groups and 23.6 percent for performance groups, and this was our recommendation to them,” he wrote.

Instead of adopting this proposal, FAST worked with MinCo to reallocate the source of MinCo groups’ supplemental funding to MinCo itself — which has its own funding pool — to alleviate some of the financial pressure on FAST, according to facilitators. “FAST felt that [the administration’s proposal] was unfair,” Greenfield said. “We are grateful to MinCo’s generosity in which we found a solution where they have now offered to help fund MinCo supplemental budgets, regardless of affiliate or core status.

FAST facilitators say they are working to amend FAST structurally to prevent future overspending and make the system more equitable. “We have paused supplemental funding for the next three weeks so that we can review our annual budgets,” Greenfield said. “In Winter Study, [we plan to] host an open constitutional convention in which RSO leaders and treasurers will be able to meet with us and discuss any potential inconveniences present in the current FAST system.”

After a constitutional convention, FAST can trigger a campus-wide referendum on proposed constitutional reforms by a vote of four of its five members.

FAST facilitators hope to make constitutional amendments to sector allocations, which have remained fixed since 2020. Competitive teams are automatically awarded 26 percent of FAST’s budget, a remnant from when FAST funded all club sports teams. Facilitators argue that this had led to an inequitable distribution of funds between RSOs. “As the current constitution is written, despite anyone’s best wishes, we are unable to reject a significantly larger budget from a competitive team than we might be able to otherwise if it came from a different sector.” Greenfield said.

“We are planning, after our constitutional convention [in January], to help redistribute funds from heftier sectors into sectors who are overburdened with more groups,” he said. “As part of this push, we are working with RSOs to cut down abnormally large annual budgets, such as the Debating Union’s budget. At the present moment, FAST is planning to cut roughly $21,000 from the Debating Union’s budget.”

According to an email from an administrator obtained by the Record, the Debating Union is disputing these planned funding cuts. Members of the administration argue that the cuts violate FAST’s constitution. FAST told the Record that they plan to move forward with the cuts, as they argue that they are important for increasing equity across RSOs.

Ultimately, FAST facilitators believe that sector reform is necessary for FAST to adequately serve the student body. “Unless sector allocations are reformed, FAST will continue to malfunction,” Greenfield said.

item.title: Marching through the history of the College’s defunct ‘military marching band’
item.dc:creator: Stella Bleiweis and Aiden Clarke
item.description: Ever wondered why the College has no Mucho Macho Moocow Military Marching Band? Read on to find out about the rise and fall of the College's historic marching band, through the Second World War and gender integration at the College, to their last performance in 2022.
item.content:encoded:
As alums gathered on Saturday at Weston Field for Homecoming, some missed a beloved tradition.

For decades, the football team could expect encouragement from the stands by chants like:

“e to the x dx dx,

e to the x dx

Cosine secant tangent sine,

Come on Williams, hold that line!”

The voices cheering from the sidelines belonged to members of the Mucho Macho Moocow Military Marching Band. Sporting purple ties and bizarre hats, the student ensemble played everything from trumpets and sousaphones to triangles and kazoos.

Unlike bands at other NESCAC schools, the College’s marching band did more than just serenade from the stands. Members of the marching band regularly took to the field for halftime performances. “We had a lot of pride that we were the only marching band in the NESCAC [on the field],” Will Harron ’11, who led the band in his junior and senior years, said in an interview with the Record.

The group’s last major performance was at Homecoming in 2022, according to former band member Kawika Tu ’26. Its once familiar parades down Spring Street and witty chants have disappeared from campus. But the band remains one of the most beloved traditions for alums.

The band’s origins stretch back nearly 100 years. A Record article published on Oct. 24, 1994, dates its beginnings to 1929.

When Professor of Music Irwin Shainman joined the faculty in 1948, he inherited a band in need of some attention, and under his direction, it began to blossom. In a 1991 interview with the Record, Shainman recalled being asked if he could revamp the College’s band while interviewing for his job. He took on the challenge with gusto.

Shainman said that he first entered a band room littered with sheet music, purple and gold capes, and battered instruments left over from the Navy V-5 program, a wartime military training program. “And from that, I was supposed to make a band,” he said. “We turned the band from a group of kind of wandering minstrels to a respectable forty, fifty, sixty, seventy-piece band.”

Under Shainman, the band was named the College’s official marching band in 1964, according to an Oct. 24, 1966 Record article.

The band’s uniforms also underwent a transformation. Anson Piper ’40 recalled in a Dec. 9, 1966, Record article that the band had a “decided inclination toward Prussian military attire.” Members wore a “purple cape with gold interior, white flannel trousers, and a hat patterned after the traditional German battle helmets,” according to Piper.

But as Shainman developed the band after World War II, its headwear became an opportunity for humor. According to Justin Brown ’05, who met Shainman during his time at the College, the former director wanted to create something less rigid than the military-style marching bands of the era. “The military was a big part of everybody’s lives,” Brown recalled in an interview with the Record. “[Shainman] wanted to do something a little … more relaxed.”

“Everybody from the neck up had to be doing something silly,” Brown said. Members still wore jackets and purple ties, but instead of matching hats, they could choose their own, a tradition that continued even as the rest of the band’s uniforms changed over the decades.

Daniel Blagden ’62, who played baritone horn in the band, recalled that the hats were a creative outlet for members. “They were our marks of individual distinction,” he said in an interview with the Record. Blagden’s own choice was a Smokey Bear hat adorned with a 1975 trout-fishing license.

By the 1970s, the band had become a prominent part of campus life. Richard Levy ’74, who played trumpet, recalled in a 2019 interview with Wendy Hopkins ’72, director of the College’s oral history program, that as many as 75 members performed in its parades during his time at the College. The group also performed at sports games and organized concerts, including one for children in Town.

Perhaps one of the band’s most memorable traditions was its parade down Spring Street before home football games. Once at the game, members practiced what they called “scrambling.” Rather than marching through carefully choreographed transitions, at halftime, they would run, literally scrambling across the field, before assembling into their next shape.

The shows were accompanied by witty skits and stories read aloud over the stadium’s public-address system, incorporating political satire, puns, and jokes about the College’s opponents.

Halftime performances traditionally concluded with the band forming a giant M for “mountain” and playing “The Mountains,” according to former members.

The arrival of the College’s first fully coeducational entering class in 1971 brought women into the band. In an interview published as part of the College’s 50+ Years of Coeducation project, Suzanne Fluhr ’75 recalled receiving a recruitment letter before she arrived on campus from Francis Cardillo, who became the band director in 1964. He wrote that she was “the first girl member” admitted to the band and hoped she would consider it “some sort of honor.”

Susan Cronin ’75, who performed with the band as a majorette during her first year at the College, recalled that the band actively encouraged women’s participation. “It was one of the most inviting [and] inclusive [groups],” she recalled in an interview with the Record.

The band’s humor sometimes took a more risqué turn. In the College’s coeducation interviews, Elizabeth Titus ’75 recalled a halftime skit in which a majorette performed a striptease parody, removing layers of clothing as the band played.

The band’s goofy spirit continued through the following decades. According to the Williams Magazine, in 1996, members presented Amherst with a $1.6 billion bill for overdue library books, poking fun at the longstanding legend that Amherst’s founders stole books from the College.

By the 1990s, the band faced challenges to its institutional support, having lost funding from the athletic department. Members were forced to seek financial support from the College Council, according to an Oct. 24, 1994, Record article.

At some point along the way, the College stopped awarding PE credit for participation in the marching band. Professor and Chair of Physics and Astronomy Charlie Doret ’02, who was in the band during his time at the College, said that the change occurred toward the end of his undergraduate years and contributed to the decline in membership.

The band was also known as a welcome alternative to the College’s more cutthroat extracurriculars. Its emphasis was on inviting everyone to join, from high school marching band veterans to people who had never picked up an instrument. The latter were given purple-and-gold kazoos monogrammed with “Williams College Marching Band” to play.

Lida Doret ’02, who played the flute in the band, recalled leaving junior varsity soccer to spend more time with her bandmates because of how welcoming they were. “You just kind of showed up as you were,” she said in an interview with the Record. “There was no expectation for who you had to be.”

Homecoming brought former members back each year to perform alongside current students. Charlie Doret, who played in the band as an undergraduate, recalled that alums would join the group for informal Saturday morning rehearsals before attending the game together.

Lida Doret remembered the returning members making Homecoming especially meaningful. “It was neat to see as a student that I was part of a bigger community, not just those who were on campus,” she said.

Among the most devoted returning members was Blagden, who estimated that he played with the band 57 times after graduating, including 54 Homecoming appearances.

For Blagden, returning to campus offered an opportunity to continue playing music while reconnecting with his former bandmates and meeting younger members. “It was just fun doing it, and seeing friends … and meeting new ones,” he said.

The hats were not the only thing that made the group distinctive. Brown described an annual tradition called “band maneuvers,” where members dressed in black and attempted to sneak into dormitories and dining halls, play a song, and escape undetected. Their attempts at stealth were complicated by the fact that some members were carrying instruments as large as sousaphones. “The whole thing was just plain silly,” Brown said. “And that was the point.”

In 2007, ESPN’s College GameDay traveled to the College for the Ephs’ Homecoming matchup against Amherst. Harron recalled that, ahead of the broadcast, a student posted on the Williams Students Online message board that the marching band had better not embarrass the College on national television.

To Harron’s surprise, football players came to the band’s defense. “Football players went on and [were] like, ‘Hey, the marching band shows up every week and plays and cheers and are there for us,’” Harron recalled. “‘They’re not an embarrassment.’”

But sustaining the band was becoming increasingly difficult, and recruitment was a persistent challenge. Harron recalled that members sometimes tried to persuade students passing by rehearsals near Frosh Quad to join, even if they had never played an instrument.

By fall 2022, membership had dwindled to approximately five students, according to Kawika Tu ’26, who participated in the band that year.

Tu recalled that the group practiced in a concrete corridor in the basement of Schapiro Hall, a far cry from the large ensemble that had once rehearsed in Chapin Hall. “The acoustics were terrible,” he wrote. “We didn’t have enough space to play facing each other, even though there were only like five of us.”

Former members pointed to several challenges that may have contributed to the band’s disappearance, including the loss of PE credit for band participation and limited institutional support. Harron recalled that once the band had become so small, convincing new students to join became difficult.

Despite the difficulties, Tu remembered the experience fondly. “There were still people who hadn’t played before, it was a goofy crew,” he wrote. “I wanted to join because everyone was so nice and smiley.”

While Harron recalled feeling pressured to conform to the College’s culture of “effortless perfection,” the marching band offered the opposite. “The marching band really was an ‘effortless imperfection,’” he said. “We got to do something that was intentionally silly, intentionally unprofessional, intentionally imperfect. And it was beautiful.”

item.title: Palantir has no place at the College: A coffee chat with a kill chain
item.dc:creator: Basim Mutaal
item.description: In an op-ed, Basim Mutaal '27 denounces Palantir's planned presence on campus and calls on students at the College to speak out against it.
item.content:encoded:
Last Friday, the ’68 Center for Career Exploration planned to host Palantir Technologies as an opportunity for students at the College to see “how software creates real-world impact.” Some of us know this “real-world impact” too well. We have friends whose families were torn apart by ICE abductions, friends who fled Palestine or had relatives killed there, and friends impacted by the attack on Iran. And yet, the College invited students to network with a company that enables this violence.

Welcoming Palantir was not a neutral act. It answered no student demand and informed no one. And, like so much here, it was decided without student input.

The administration calls its decision not to take institutional positions on world events “neutrality,” and claims to merely give students the information needed for a decision rather than making it for them. I agree, except students were never provided this information when the “real-world impact” of Palantir’s work was conveniently left out of the publicity material. At best, the College let the company write its own introduction without any pushback, and at worst, they tried to launder the company’s reputation.

The College rolled out the red carpet for Palantir, while vetoing student proposals to invite certain authors to Claiming Williams Day, a day meant for all of us to make this place our own. Choosing who, and whose speech, is welcome is gatekeeping, and it is not neutral. It sanctions one kind of speech and that is a political stance in itself. We cannot claim the College, but Palantir can.

This gatekeeping is ingrained in the structure of the College. For example, the committee that revised the College’s protest and posting policies in 2024 had only two students and five faculty and staff. On this year’s Claiming Williams steering committee, students hold a mere three out of 15 seats. Errors made by the Title IX office that jeopardized student safety had to be exposed by students themselves. Time and time again, we are consulted last and overruled first.

The lack of student input and bureaucracy was just as true in the case of the Palantir event. One of the potential speakers for the protest told us, organizers from the Concerned Students’ Collective (CSC), that administrators had advised them not to speak. Staff members even warned us of possible private security at the Palantir event, like at Cornell, where Palantir made students show ID and sign a nondisclosure agreement while campus police were posted in the hallways.

Amid the administration’s radio silence, the ’68 Center agreed to talk when we, organizers from the CSC, showed up at its door. There, we met six directors and staff and were told that “we were preaching to the choir.” One of them admitted they hadn’t known how bad the company was until they read our statement online.

We were told the ’68 Center only turns a prospective employer away over reports of sexual assault or abuse, yet its own guidelines reserve “the right to reject any job or internship posting.” Their hands were never tied. We were also told that the ’68 Center was looking into amending that policy. However, a policy rewritten without student involvement will fail the same way. When alums wrote in to the ’68 Center, one of its directors replied, “We did not invite Palantir to campus.” But the ’68 Center planned to host Palantir, sent out a campus-wide email, and lent it the College’s space, visibility, and name. Arguing over who called whom is how an institution dodges responsibility and avoids the principle argument.

The College knows exactly which careers it wants credit for. It presents itself to the world as a bastion of progressive thinking, and its social media profiles almost exclusively celebrate alumni at nonprofits and environmental organizations. It then simultaneously opens its doors to a company that gives governments and organizations the power to surveil and to kill. We have yet to see the College publicly celebrate an alum building civilian-targeting software. The College wants the facade of humanitarian progress on Instagram, while managing a recruiting pipeline for a company which offers soldiers, in its own words, “an AI-powered kill chain.”

Hosting recruiters like this isn’t new, and students at the College have been here before. In 1985, students protesting the war against Nicaragua tried to place a visiting CIA recruiter under “citizen’s arrest.” Since then the College has continued to host recruiters implicated in human rights violations and violence. Except now, the recruiter is funded by a CIA-backed venture capital firm, In-Q-Tel, and helped the National Security Agency and its Five Eyes partners sift intercepted internet data. Previous generations of students refused to let the surveillance state recruit here, and we cannot be the ones who welcome it over pizza and coffee. This isn’t partisan, and you do not need to share the CSC’s politics to see the problem.

The College’s mission states that it aspires to send students out with “a firm desire to lead lives of meaning and purpose.” Students practiced exactly that when 70 percent of them voted for fossil-fuel divestment in 2015, when they blocked CIA recruiting interviews, and when they camped on Sawyer Quad in a call for the College to divest from weapons manufacturers. Too often, the College has answered students’ clear demands with vague committees, policies, and refusals. But, ultimately, a college exists for its students. It is our theses, our activism, and our careers that the College gets to boast about.

The College owes its prestige to its students. It owes us better than a coffee chat with the kill chain. It tells us to become engaged members of our communities, yet stonewalls us when we do. It keeps alienating us — through breaking Title IX policies, undermining TAPSI housing, controlling the speakers we can invite, and projecting a facade of neutrality. Its first responsibility is to its students, not to a company’s recruiting pipeline.

Eventually, it was Palantir that postponed its visit, not the College. Palantir has since continued to recruit by email, offering students one-on-one calls and acknowledging “a complicated moment on campus.”

So our demands stand: First, cut the College’s ties to Palantir, from on-campus recruiting to Winter Study trips to its offices as recently as 2025, and guarantee it will not return to campus. Second, no policy changes without substantial, non-symbolic student involvement.

On Friday, Bolin Weekend panelists offered to cancel their talks, engaged objectors wrote in concerns, and over 100 students, alums, faculty, staff, and neighbors stood at Mears House to say our demands out loud. And will keep saying it. We, the CSC, also ask every student to speak up again and again and again. Do it peacefully, do it loudly, and do it together for causes you believe in. Generations of Ephs refused to let the College be used this way. We won’t either.

Not in our name.

Basim Mutaal ’27 is a computer science, political science, and economics major from Lahore, Pakistan.

item.title: Renowned pianist Orion Weiss critiques students in masterclass
item.dc:creator: Eliana Rosner and Maya Ventakesh
item.description: In front of a packed Brooks-Rogers Recital Hall, four piano students at the College performed a classical piece onstage for acclaimed concert pianist Orion Weiss on Wednesday, Nov. 11.
item.content:encoded:
In front of a packed Brooks-Rogers Recital Hall, four piano students at the College each performed a classical piece onstage for acclaimed concert pianist Orion Weiss last Wednesday. 

Described as a “brilliant pianist” by The New York Times, Weiss has performed at premier concert halls such as Carnegie Hall, Lincoln Center, London’s Wigmore Hall, and the Kennedy Center. He has also performed with all of the American “big five” orchestras.

What unfolded on Wednesday evening felt more like a public piano lesson than a performance: Each student played a classical piano piece from composers such as Beethoven, Chopin, and Schubert, and then received verbal critique from Weiss. This structure of public performance and subsequent critique is known as a masterclass.

Weiss focused primarily on emotion rather than technique in his critique. With enthusiasm and commentary that occasionally elicited laughs from the audience, he took each student through their piece, listening, playing, and singing along. 

Weiss became so immersed in the music that Director of Keyboard Studies Jeewon Park, who had invited him, had to let him know that he was running over time. 

Despite being such a renowned pianist, Weiss taught in a down-to-earth manner, using lighthearted yet astute metaphors to help his students capture feelings and phrasing in their work.

Weiss and Park are longtime colleagues. “I have always had this long admiration for his musicianship,” Park said in an interview with the Record. “When I first began my work here, I immediately thought of him because of his approach to music. And that was so apparent during [the masterclass].” 

Weiss said that he focuses on supporting students when he teaches, similarly to how he practices piano himself. “[My teaching style] is trying to be encouraging. We’re all in the same path, trying to make this music meaningful, and … to  bond with it in the way we can,” Weiss said in an interview with the Record.

Park vouched for Weiss’ positive approach. “He’s one of the most kind and generous and thoughtful people that I have ever met,” she said. “So I had no doubt that his class was going to be positive and supportive and inspiring.”

Weiss directed attention away from the audience, treating the masterclass like a one-on-one lesson, a technique that draws upon his own favorable experiences as a student. “Some of my favorite masterclasses were not by me, but teachers who would get up and say amazing, interesting, profound things about the pieces and historical background,” Weiss said. “I really just feel like the best I can do is take the time to help the student with whatever ideas I have, and the audience are just our observers to that.”

Rosie Heghinian ’29, a pianist who watched the masterclass, said the event provided a unique connection to musicians outside of the College. “I think it’s incredible to have practicing pianists who are active in their local music scene, like from New York and similar places, come to campus,” she said. “Our music professors are so entrenched in that world, but it’s a side of them that we don’t get to see, so it puts the music department into context a little bit… It’s just amazing to have this kind of person on campus.” 

Three of the four students who performed are studying piano with Park and have been practicing their pieces since the summer. Park highlighted the freedom she gives her students in their work. “I wanted to give them total agency in what they want to study,” she said. “I am also very impressed with the level of repertoire that they chose, because it is advanced.”

Heghinian was struck by Weiss’s emphasis on expression. “His teaching style was more rooted in playing. It was more like a follow-after-me kind of thing, more about imitation and repetition, which I wasn’t expecting,” she said. “I was expecting [him] to be, like, ‘Play it this way,’ and give them precise adjectives. He would model it, and they would use their ears, so it was very aural kind of learning, which I thought was fascinating.”

Yet Weiss’s positivity, especially in classical piano, which is a field of music that is often associated with rigid technique and obsessive practicing, created an openness to the masterclass environment as a whole. “Every musician has a different approach to teaching, so I like the idea of bringing in as much of that world as we can and navigating different pianists approaches to teaching, and how they play, and how that translates into how students play,” Heghinian said. “I think it’s awesome to have someone like that on campus.”

Being publicly critiqued, especially by such a prominent musician, could certainly be intimidating for students, according to Park. “Masterclasses can be tricky,” she said. “You don’t have that much time, so you’re there to get this big picture.” 

Nevertheless, she believed her students were up for the challenge. “They’re very secure, very centered,” she said.

She also stressed that the goal is not to create a perfect performance. “We’re not here to make perfect expressions, because we are all human. Even these pieces are written by humans,” Park said. “It’s about expressing a wide range of human emotions, so if [the piece] is perfect, we’re not really doing it right.”

item.title: Football falls to Amherst at Homecoming
item.dc:creator: Kaileen So
item.description: Football (5-4) fell to the Amherst Mammoths (8-1) 16-7 at Farley-Lamb Field on Saturday in the Ephs’ Homecoming game and the “Biggest Little Game in America.” Heading into the matchup, the Ephs understood the significance of the game given the College’s longtime rivalry with Amherst. “We play a lot into the tradition of the Williams-Amherst...
item.content:encoded:
Football (5-4) fell to the Amherst Mammoths (8-1) 16-7 at Farley-Lamb Field on Saturday in the Ephs’ Homecoming game and the “Biggest Little Game in America.”

Heading into the matchup, the Ephs understood the significance of the game given the College’s longtime rivalry with Amherst. “We play a lot into the tradition of the Williams-Amherst rivalry,” running back Matt Bott ’28 said. “We just wanted to honor the tradition, so we did everything we could during practice to come up with a successful game.”

For the team’s seniors, the game, the last of the season, carried added significance as their final opportunity to take the field together. “Senior Day is emotional,” quarterback Drew Renzella ’27 said. “Some of my best friends are on the team. So it means a lot… Everyone has that on their mind to put their best foot forward in the last game.”

Both teams got off to a slow offensive start during the first quarter. The Ephs were unable to convert a first down, and the Mammoths were held scoreless despite entering Ephs territory on each of their possessions.

The Ephs’ defense continued to hold strong throughout the afternoon, keeping the game close. “Our defense did a great job at limiting their offense,” Bott said. “Our offense had a tough time out there, but our defense kept us in it for the most part.”

The second quarter opened with the Mammoths facing fourth-and-8 at the Ephs’ 36-yard line. Electing to go for it, the Mammoths converted on an 18-yard reception to enter the red zone. A rush by Mammoths running back Zachary Curtin secured the Mammoths a touchdown, giving them a 7-0 lead just over a minute into the quarter.

The Ephs responded on their next possession, starting with a decisive 13-yard run by wide receiver Brady Stahelski ’27. Two plays later, a facemask penalty against the Mammoths brought the Ephs into opposing territory for the first time that day.

A series of runs from four different Ephs advanced the team past the Mammoths’ 20-yard line, with a 3-yard touchdown run from Bott capping off the drive to tie the game at 7-7.

With the score remaining level through the end of the second quarter, the Ephs hoped to maintain their steady offensive rhythm heading into the second half. “The mindset was to stay on the path, and continue to run the ball, get first downs, get completions, and string plays together into a drive,” Renzella said. “With the tie game, the focus was one play at a time.”

The defensive battle continued into the third quarter, with both teams forcing two consecutive three-and-outs to open the half.

Halfway through the quarter, the Mammoths completed a 42-yard pass to reach the Ephs’ 20-yard line, but the Ephs successfully prevented the Mammoths from reaching the end zone, forcing the visitors to settle for a 29-yard field goal for a 10-7 lead.

On their next possession, the Ephs advanced into Mammoths territory following two strong rushes from Owen McHugh ’27 and Stahelski. But an illegal substitution penalty and a rush for negative yardage left the Ephs facing a fourth-and-16 to open the fourth quarter, which the team was unable to convert.

The Mammoths then took over and marched down the field to the Ephs’ 3-yard line, until a forced fumble from linebacker Luke Mangini ’28 halted their drive. Despite the turnover, the Ephs were unable to gain positive yardage on their ensuing possession and were forced to punt the ball from deep in their own territory, giving the Mammoths favorable field position.

After advancing to the Ephs’ 16-yard line, Mammoths quarterback Marek Hill fired a contested pass into the end zone, towards Mammoths receiver Christian Moore and co-captain and cornerback Holden Gering ’27. “I jumped in the air, intercepted the pass, and secured the football, while falling to the ground on my back,” Gering wrote. “The opposing receiver climbed on top of me and tried to bear hug the ball.”

However, the Mammoths were ultimately awarded the touchdown after a struggle for the ball, extending their lead to 16-7 after a missed extra point with under four minutes left in the game.

Despite the blow to their momentum, the Ephs came out strong on the next drive, with Renzella completing three consecutive passes to bring the team past midfield. The drive stalled at the Mammoths’ 15-yard line after a couple incomplete passes brought up fourth-and-4. The Ephs decided to go for it, but Renzella’s pass was picked off by a Mammoths defender. Then, with just over a minute left, the Mammoths secured the first down needed to run out the clock and seal their 16-7 win.

The Ephs have lost three out of their last four games, a falloff from their 4-1 record earlier in the season. However, Renzella emphasized that the team’s record did not fully reflect its performance. “It’s tough to think about the season in terms of the record,” he said. “I’m really proud of how everyone stepped up when they needed to, and how we showed toughness at times of adversity.”

The Ephs have faced numerous injuries throughout the season, starting four different quarterbacks across nine games. Despite these challenges, Bott emphasized the importance of having players who are always ready to step into larger roles. “We’ve always had that … mentality where even our second- and third-string guys know that at any moment they could be put in the game,” he said. “We all practice like we’re going to be the ones out there on game day, and that leads to us having a lot of depth at every position.”

Though the Ephs have wrapped up their season, Gering remains optimistic about the team’s future. “The level of maturity and buy-in that many of the underclassmen developed as the season went along makes me very confident,” he wrote. “They have an extraordinary opportunity ahead of them to achieve a high level of success in the years to come because they are not only talented, but they are more importantly willing to sacrifice anything for the collective goal of success.”

item.title: One in Two Thousand: Alex De Biasio ’28
item.dc:creator: Audrey Adam
item.description: Each week, the Record (using a script in R) randomly selects a student at the College for our One in Two Thousand feature, excluding current Record board members. This week, Alex De Biasio ’28 discussed his interests in mathematics and music composition, his love for hiking, and how the two intersect. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.
item.content:encoded:
Each week, the Record (using a script in R) randomly selects a student at the College for our One in Two Thousand feature, excluding current Record board members. This week, Alex De Biasio ’28 discussed his interests in mathematics and music composition, his love for hiking, and how the two intersect. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Audrey Adam (AA): I know you study math. Do you prefer applied or pure math?

Alex De Biasio (AD): I’m conflicted. I’ve done so much pure math since I got here. It’s been the foundation of basically every class besides “Probability.” The problem is that pure math is not useful for jobs, so I’ve been taking more statistics classes recently. But in terms of enjoyment, I do really enjoy the act of doing math for its own sake, which is maybe why I’m drawn to abstract math.

AA: I saw that you’re TA-ing “Topology” this semester. When did you take that course?

AD: Yeah, I took that my freshman year with [Associate Professor of Mathematics] Leo Goldmakher.

AA: Wow, “Topology,” a 400-level course, your freshman year?

AD: Yeah.

AA: Oh my god, I’m clutching my pearls. And you enjoyed it?

AD: [Laughs.] Yeah. It was so good because Professor Goldmakher is very, very unique in his teaching style, in my opinion. He has the class collectively discover the results rather than teaching them to us. Often, we would say things that weren’t quite right, then run with them and see what happened during class. It was really worthwhile.

AA: And have you taken “Real Analysis”? My friends who are in it are always stressed out.

AD: Yeah, I actually took it before I got here. I’m definitely stronger in algebra than I am in real analysis. This semester, I’m taking a sequel to real analysis, “Harmonic Analysis Through Music.”

AA: Wow. “Harmonic Analysis Through Music.” Do you play music outside of school?

AD: Yeah. Right now, I’m doing a lot of music stuff. I’m taking piano lessons, and I’m also part of choir. And I just do random accompaniments in general.

AA: Do you prefer a certain genre of piano, like classical or jazz?

AD: Yeah, I definitely prefer classical. I did some jazz in high school, but I’ve had a lot of classical training, so it’s where I’m most comfortable.

AA: If you could have a dinner party with one composer, dead or alive, who would it be?

AD: It’s hard to say, but I think I would choose Samuil Feinberg. He wrote 12 piano sonatas, and they’re all really, really interesting. He was inspired by Alexander Scriabin and took his harmonic language and blended it with Bach’s counterpoint. The result is insane. Some of the piano music is impossible to play. Not only that, but I also think the sounds he gets from the piano are very interesting.

AA: Do you compose?

AD: I used to compose a lot. I took two composition classes at the College, and I used to do it all the time in high school. I’ve done it since I was 10, actually. I have a profile on Online Sequencer, where you can place notes on a grid and hear them back. So I experimented with that, and made like 900 small compositions since I was 10.

AA: I know there’s a growing body of mathematics specific to music theory. Is this something you’re interested in?

AD: I guess I sometimes think of playing music mathematically. Not explicitly, but, for instance, when I’m learning a piano piece, I’ll often run through it in my head, and if I get to a place where I’m not sure what the notes are, I’ll derive them from what’s around them and then think, where does the music need to go, and how can it get there. Of course, it doesn’t always follow the rules, but I sometimes think of it like a logic puzzle when I’m unsure what is happening. And then I also use math to remember intervals by breaking them down into smaller intervals.

AA: I heard that you go on hikes with the Williams Outing Club. How did you get involved in it?

AD: It started freshman year when I was just looking for community. I signed up at the Purple Key Fair, and they sent me emails from then on. It seemed like something I should take advantage of while I’m at the College. I feel like it would be so sad to be next to this nature and not do anything about it. Part of the reason I got into hiking is that during the COVID-19 pandemic, my dad and I would go hiking every weekend. We would challenge ourselves to go fast, with as much elevation gain as possible.

AA: Before we finish, I have a question I ask all my friends who study math. It’s a “kiss, marry, kill” question.

AD: [Laughs.] Okay.

AA: Ready? Groups, fields, and rings.

AD: Oh man. I can definitely say I would kill the field, then probably marry the ring, and kiss the group.

AA: And why?

AD: I think rings have such an interesting structure. I don’t like fields because they’re so constrained that I feel they’re less interesting than rings. But groups are just groups, so it’s like, okay, whatever. But rings, if you look at what [Professor of Mathematics] Susan Loepp is doing, she’s constructing the weirdest rings with the most random properties that somehow work out. And you don’t have that for groups. Groups are great, but not as good as rings.

AA: I guess it’s fitting that you would marry a ring, since you’d be putting a ring on it.

AD: Yeah, that is very fitting. [Laughs.]

item.title: Three Spring Street businesses close, relocate
item.dc:creator: Cara Huang and Kaileen So
item.description: In a Spring Street shakeup, Plates Mediterranean Bistro permanently closed on Nov. 8, the Tea & Boba Lounge will close next month, and Nature’s Closet is moving to a new location across the street. The owners of all three establishments cited financial concerns as a primary factor behind their decisions.
item.content:encoded:
In a Spring Street shakeup, Plates Mediterranean Bistro permanently closed on Nov. 8, the Tea & Boba Lounge will close next month, and Nature’s Closet is moving to a new location across the street. The owners of all three establishments cited financial concerns as a primary factor behind their decisions.

Plates Mediterranean Bistro permanently closes

Plates, which closed on Nov. 8, was also temporarily closed last winter, when the bistro underwent renovations and a menu revamp.

Plates opened in 2013 as Pera. It was renamed two years ago in reference to the Turkish plates that decorated the restaurant’s interior. The restaurant served both lunch and dinner seven days a week and offered a menu that included salads, flatbreads, pasta, and grilled meats.

Co-owner Mel Sari cited difficulties securing consistent staffing due in part to the region’s high cost of living as a factor behind the restaurant’s closure. She also pointed to declining opportunities for local businesses, namely the College’s shift toward outside catering companies for major events and the absence of the Williamstown Theatre Festival (WTF) this summer. “Consequently, local restaurants do not benefit from visitor traffic during the area’s peak week,” Sari wrote to the Record.

In a message posted on Plates’ website titled “A Heartfelt Goodbye,” co-owner Ahri Frank called for greater support for local businesses. “I hope that the town leadership will become more business oriented and take initiatives to organize events that bring visitors, attract tourists, and create more opportunities for local businesses to thrive,” he wrote.

Tea & Boba Lounge to permanently close

The Tea & Boba Lounge’s last day of operation will be Dec. 6 due to rising business operation costs and fewer customers, according to owner Glory-Anne Jones. With her three-year lease ending this year, Jones said that she decided to permanently close up shop.

“It’s really a lack of revenue… With the economy as it is, I think that boba and cookies are the last on people’s list of things to spend money on,” Jones told the Record. “The output did not equal the input.”

Jones also cited the effect on revenue from WTF’s change to a biennial schedule on the shop’s revenue. According to Jones, the festival brought many customers into the shop that her business relied on during the summer.

Jones said that some of her favorite memories of running Tea & Boba Lounge include the Rolodex in the store that holds regular customers’ orders and giving talks to students at the College about her travels to Nepal, where she took a tea tour.

Nature’s Closet to move

After approximately 12 years at 61 Spring Street, outdoor store Nature’s Closet is set to move across the street to 40 Spring Street, a spot that has been newly renovated since the closure of Purple Dragon Games in 2023. The store will remain open through Christmas Eve, before relocating during the week between Christmas Eve and New Year’s Day, with hopes of reopening around Jan. 2, according to owner Amy Jeschawitz.

This move to a more affordable space will allow the store to remain financially sustainable while continuing to serve the Town, according to Jeschawitz. “The town needs a shop like this in our community,” she said in an interview with the Record. “Making this choice to move is so that I’m able to keep all my employees employed and keep the shop open.”

For Jeschawitz, maintaining the store’s presence on Spring Street is particularly important amid recent business closures. “I think the economics in Town have changed,” she said. “We don’t have as many retail establishments as we used to and that’s kind of the thing [that] people are looking for when they come to Town… I think that’s something that we miss.”

The College owns nine of the 20 buildings on Spring Street, including the space that the Tea and Boba Lounge occupies. Administrators are currently in talks with the Williamstown Chamber of Commerce and local entrepreneurs to identify possible businesses that would benefit from a Spring Street location, Special Assistant to the President Gina Puc and Associate Provost Chris Winters wrote in a joint statement to the Record.

The pair described the search’s priorities. “[We] want businesses that add to the vibrancy of the street and complement the mix of the products and services offered on it,” Puc and Winters wrote. “Having a lively and useful main street makes Williamstown a more attractive place to study and to work.”

item.title: Captain’s Corner: Bria Abbiati ’27
item.dc:creator: Hannah Marx
item.description: Team: Women’s soccer Hometown: Newton, Mass. Major: History and philosophy This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Hannah Marx (HM): You just won the NESCAC championship — congrats! What is your favorite moment from the season? Bria Abbiati (BA): It’s hard to say that anything besides winning the NESCAC championship was my favorite...
item.content:encoded:
Team: Women’s soccer

Hometown: Newton, Mass.

Major: History and philosophy

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

Hannah Marx (HM): You just won the NESCAC championship — congrats! What is your favorite moment from the season?

Bria Abbiati (BA): It’s hard to say that anything besides winning the NESCAC championship was my favorite moment from the season because it was a goal we’ve been building towards for so long. It’s a really memorable accomplishment, especially to win it at home. But I think second to that would be beating Middlebury in our last regular season game. It was a really gritty game. They’re a good team, and we just pulled through, which is why we got to host the NESCAC tournament. It was a really big deal to have a couple more games on Cole Field.

HM: Do you have any fun team traditions?

BA: We have a lot of fun team traditions, but one of my favorites is dancing and singing in the locker room before every game. Whether you want to be hyped up or focused, it’s so fun. It’s a way to connect, and remind each other that we’re a team, we’re excited for the game, and we’re lucky to be there before we step out onto the field. That’s something that I look forward to every week. It helps take my mind off the pressure of soccer.

HM: I always see your team in minions gear on Instagram. Can you tell me about them?

BA: Credit to Elle Long [’28] for spearheading the minion project. Our 2025 intramural basketball team was called Steal the Moon. We all showed up in minion shirts, our coach was Gru, and someone was Vector as well. And we won the championship. It was the best moment ever. Since then, it’s continued and grown. I think it doesn’t even matter at this point if we fully understand every facet of the minion joke, but it’s something that we all can participate in and have a lot of fun with.

HM: On another note, why did you want to play soccer at the College?

BA: I knew I wanted to play soccer in college since I had any inkling that I might be good enough to play in college. I love the sport. It’s been a big part of my life for a really long time, and both my parents played sports at Bowdoin, so I knew that the NESCAC was an amazing place to do it. I think that Williams has been one of the best decisions I’ve made in my life. It’s a great level of soccer, and I couldn’t ask for better teammates.

HM: That’s awesome. How did you get into soccer in the first place?

BA: My mom forced me into it. She put me into kindergarten soccer, and I hated it. I would lead my kindergarten soccer team into the woods to go look for inchworms, and my mom had to usher us back and reprimand me for taking my whole team off the field and not playing because I didn’t want to play soccer. I quit soccer in second grade and then my mom forced me back into it in third grade. I just stuck with it from then on.

HM: What do you think you’ll miss most about the team after you graduate?

BA: Competing on a team takes up a lot of time at the College, but it’s also a real way to de-stress and have two hours out of your day that you cannot be thinking about anything besides your sport. You’re playing the sport that you love with your best friends at the most beautiful field. I’m going to miss getting to walk down to Cole Field at 4 p.m., put my backpack down, hang out with my friends, and play soccer every single day.

HM: What advice would you give to your first-year self just starting out?

BA: Probably to take some of the pressure off. I definitely had high expectations for myself as a player and a student, and I dealt with some injuries. I would tell her, “It’s gonna be okay. It’s your freshman fall. It’s not the end of the world if things don’t go your way, just try and enjoy it. Take the pressure off.” There’s too much pressure at this school.

HM: What do you think you’ve learned the most from being a captain?

BA: Coming into senior year, it was always in the back of my mind that this is my last season of soccer, and I want to do as well as I possibly can, but I also need to enjoy it. I’ve learned that energy, especially from the leaders, really permeates throughout the team. If people are not in a good mood, it is felt, so my lesson was just to lead by example. I think that if you have happy leaders and happy people, things can’t go that poorly.

item.title: Students, alums celebrate Sandra Burton at Bolin weekend
item.dc:creator: Aiden Clarke
item.description: Bolin Weekend is an annual event honoring the black experience at the College. This year, Senior Lecturer and Director of the Dance Department Sandra Burton was honored in a spontaneous ceremony planned by alums and current students.
item.content:encoded:
Sandra Burton, senior lecturer and director of the dance department, did not expect to be the center of attention at Friday night’s opening program for Bolin Legacy Mentorship Weekend. But the students and alums who gathered at the ’62 Center for Theatre and Dance had other plans.

“The alumni and current students are very sneaky people,” Burton said in an interview with the Record. Organizers kept their plans to honor Burton’s 43 years at the College a secret, surprising her with tributes from generations of students she had taught.

The celebration was part of Bolin Legacy Mentorship Weekend, a biennial gathering honoring Gaius Charles Bolin Sr., class of 1889, who was the College’s first Black graduate. “The weekend is centered on the Black Williams experience, celebrating the scholarship, leadership, creativity, mentorship, and community that have shaped it,” its website states.

This year’s programming, held from Nov. 13 to Nov. 15, was organized by Bishoy Yacoub ’23 and Jallicia Jolly ’14, co-chairs of the Williams Black Alumni Network (WBAN), alongside the Bolin Weekend steering committee, which is composed of alums and WBAN members, and College staff and student leaders.

Friday night’s opening program, “Because of Bolin,” brought students, alums, faculty, and staff together to celebrate the “history, legacy, and future of Black life at Williams,” according to the program’s website. The evening featured performances from the College’s Gospel Choir, Sankofa step team, hip-hop dance group NBC, and African dance and music ensemble Kusika, with alums returning to perform with current students.

WBAN also hosted “The Road to Bolin,” a virtual series held from Oct. 14 to Nov. 6 that explored topics such as identity, mentorship, and professional life, giving students and alums an opportunity to connect before Bolin Weekend.

Jolly said the series was intended to cultivate relationships across generations before they gathered in person. “We wanted to bring people across generations, across geographies, and across all barriers to be able to build relationships organically,” she said in an interview with the Record.

Beyond bringing people together, Jolly said Bolin Weekend was an opportunity to celebrate Black leadership and to ensure that their legacy continues to shape future generations. “Professor Burton embodies that through her teaching and instruction, through her mentorship and the way she builds community through dance, and also through the way she has nurtured generations of Ephs across the decades,” she said.

Burton first came to the College as a member of choreographer Chuck Davis’ dance company. The company had been invited to the College for a yearlong residency by Joy Dewey, who founded the College’s dance program within the physical education department. During the residency, Burton taught dance at both the College and local schools.

Although she initially struggled to adapt to the College’s cold weather and the difficulties of living without a car, Burton said she found a supportive community among the College’s students, faculty, and staff. “The community of color was exceptionally generous and supportive,” she said. “I ended up making lifelong friends here.”

Over the following decades, Burton became central to the dance scene at the College and co-founded Kusika in 1986.

Jolly explained how Burton’s mentorship extended outside the classroom. After her first year at the College, Jolly did summer research on campus, recalling that Burton and her husband would take her to local cultural events, introducing her to the region’s Black artistic history. “I just never forgot being 19 and exploring the Berkshires through the lens of Black legacy and Black artists,” Jolly said. “It gave me a different connection to the space, and I never forgot that.”

In her senior year, Jolly enrolled in Burton’s dance class. She said the course taught her not only about the history and culture of dance, but also about identity. “She didn’t teach us just about dance,” Jolly said. “She taught us about confidence.”

“Why do you shrink yourself in your body?” Jolly recalled Burton asking her students. “That was a question that stuck with my spirit and my soul because it reminded me that I can take up space.”

Reflecting on her time at the College, Burton emphasized the importance of continuing to grow and learn from the past. “In the 43 years that I have been present at Williams, I have experienced myself and the College attempt to grow and attempt to learn and attempt to understand,” she said. “History is the past, present, and future, and it is all around us all the time. Sometimes we are able to do great things and make change, and sometimes we stumble. And when we stumble, the test is always how we get up.”

Burton said Friday’s celebration was especially moving. “It was a delightful and inspiring experience to see both people that I have taught and people that I am teaching and collaborating with,” she said.

The evening concluded with students Burton had taught and mentored presenting her with 43 flowers, one for each year she had spent at the College. “We wanted to give her flowers quite literally,” Yacoub said.

For Yacoub, Burton’s legacy reflected the very purpose of the weekend. “Gaius Charles Bolin helped open a door for generations of students,” he said. “Sandra Burton made what lies beyond that door a place where students can celebrate who they are.”
